drills.title: vs xarav973 (841) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: White wanted Rxd3, so your queen has to leave d3 or make its move count. Qxa3 wins a pawn but walks off the d-file, so Qxf5 can now take the f5 pawn your queen had been guarding through e4, and White's rooks start to wake up. You were nearly seven pawns up, and this grab gives back about two. Qxd1 is the move: you take the rook, and after Qxf7+ Kxf7 Rxd1 the queens are traded and you finish about the exchange ahead. Before grabbing material, ask what your queen was guarding and what is attacking it.
drills.threat: White's rook on d1 is lined up straight down the d-file on your queen on d3.

drills.title: vs xarav973 (841) — Scotch Game
drills.coachNote: Ng5 would put the knight on h7 and f7 and make Qxh7 a mating idea against your king on g8. Bf6 looks sturdy, but after Ng5 Bxg5 Qxg5 the f4 push kicks the queen and White's attack keeps rolling. You were nearly seven pawns up, and this retreat hands back about 1.6 of them along with the initiative. Bxf2+ is the move: it takes a pawn with check, and after Kh1 the bishop on e6 slides to f7, hitting the queen on h5. When the queen runs to g5, Bxe1 wins the rook, and Rxe1 leaves you a rook and a pawn for a bishop.
drills.threat: White's knight wants to jump to g5, and with his queen on h5 aimed at h7, that's a mating attack.

drills.title: vs AlfredoPig (770) — Four Knights Game Double Spanish Variation
drills.coachNote: White's knight wants f5, and his queen wants a say on the queenside. Qb6 steps onto a5's diagonal to offer a queen trade, and after Nf5 you are defending instead of attacking, which costs about four pawns of swing from a level position. Qe3 is stronger: it hits the knight on g3 along the third rank and the rook on c1 along the e3-d2-c1 diagonal, so White can't meet both. After Qxc7 Qxd3+ you win a pawn back with check, and Rd7 chases the white queen to e5. Look for the square that hits two targets at once.
drills.threat: White's queen on a5 eyes your b5 pawn, and his knight on g3 is heading for f5 to hit g7.

drills.title: vs AlfredoPig (770) — Four Knights Game Double Spanish Variation
drills.coachNote: White's knight is heading to g3, and the real fight is between your c4 pawn and his d3 pawn. a5 looks like a harmless flank push, but a6 was the only pawn guarding b5, so a4 wins that pawn and your edge melts. You were slightly better at +1.2, and this push gives back about 2.4 pawns of it. cxd3 is the move: after Ng3 dxc2+ Qxc2 Rxd1+ Rxd1 the rooks come off and you finish a pawn up. Before you push a pawn, check which pawn it was quietly defending.
drills.threat: White's knight is about to reroute to g3, and the c4-d3 pawn tension is coming to a head.

drills.title: vs Wuranti (790) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black has two pieces aimed at your bishop on d3, and your queen on d1 is its only guard. Qb3 still guards d3 along the third rank, but it leaves the d-file, and after Bxd3 Nxa7 Kxa7 Qxb4 the account is only partly settled, so you have given up about four pawns from level. Rc7 is the move: it hits the queen on d7 with a rook she can't simply ignore. The forced line that follows, Qxc7 Nxc7 Bxd3 Re1 Kxc7, is the least bad way to keep the balance, and the engine prefers it to anything quieter.
drills.threat: Black's knight on b4 and bishop on g6 both bear on your bishop on d3, which only your queen defends.

drills.title: vs Wuranti (790) — London System
drills.coachNote: Black wants to trade on f4 with the d6 bishop, while the g6 bishop stares at your d3 bishop. Bh2 steps your bishop out of the d6 bishop's line, but it allows Bxh2+ with check, and after Kxh2 and Kb8 the knight jumps to e5 and forks the queen on d7 with the g6 bishop and the c6 knight. You were up about four and a half pawns, and this retreat gives back roughly 3.6 of them. Nb5 is the move: it hits the bishop on d6 before it can take on f4, and if Bxf4 exf4 comes, Nxa7+ wins a pawn with check. The principle is to attack the piece that is tying yours down, not run from it.
drills.threat: Black's bishop on d6 lines up on your bishop on f4, and his bishop on g6 eyes your bishop on d3 along the diagonal.

drills.coachNote: Black has two ideas: Bxe5 to trade your bishop, and Rxc3 down the open c-file against a pawn nobody defends. Qe1 guards neither target, so after Bxe5 dxe5 the queen swings to c7 and hits both e5 and c3, and f4 can only guard one. You were up about 1.3 pawns, and this move turns that into a slight deficit. Bf4 is the move: the bishop steps off the g7 diagonal to a square where it stays active, and after Rxc3 Qd2 hits the rook. Giving up the c3 pawn to keep the bishop and the c-file is the right trade here.
drills.threat: Black's bishop on g7 is lined up on your bishop on e5, and his rook on c8 is aimed at your c3 pawn.

drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: What White wanted was Rb8+, a check along the eighth rank that leaves you only Nc8 as a block, with the d6 and e6 pawns controlling the squares your king would need. Going to d8 walks straight into that: after Rb8+ Nc8 c6 and Rh7 you lose the tempo race, and the swing takes you from -2.7 to about -10.6. Kc8 is the answer because the king sits next to b8, so Rb8+ just drops the rook to Kxb8. From there the best line keeps you fighting, with c6 and Rb7+ as White's ideas but nothing decisive. The principle: before you step toward a square, list every check your opponent has on it.
drills.threat: White's rook on b6 is eyeing b8 with check, and his d6 and e6 pawns are crowding the squares around your king.

drills.title: vs fantagalo (819) — Ruy Lopez Opening
drills.coachNote: What White wanted was Rxc5, winning the c5 pawn while the c-file is open and nothing defends it. Kd7 does nothing to stop that, and after Rc8 the e6+ fork drives your king to d8 while White's pawns keep rolling. You were level at -0.1, so this costs you about three pawns. Nxd5 instead grabs the loose d5 pawn with your knight from e7, and when Rxc5+ checks you block with Rc7 and trade rooks on c6, staying level. The principle: when a rook lines up on an open file, check which of its targets are defended before you spend a move elsewhere.
drills.threat: White's rook on c1 is lined up on the open c-file against your c5 pawn, while his d and e pawns press forward.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: You had a mate here, not a pawn: Qg2 slides your queen from c6 down the long diagonal, defended by the rook on f2, and White's king on g1 has nowhere to go. Rxb2 grabs a pawn instead, and after Nd2 the knight blocks the rook's second-rank line, so Qc2 and Rh2 fizzle and the attack evaporates. You were winning by about 20 pawns, and this throws away roughly 15 of that. Qg2 ends the game on the spot, since Kxg2 is illegal and f1 and h2 are covered. The principle: before you take material, check for a mate in one, because the pawn will still be there afterwards and the mate will not.
drills.threat: White's queen on g5 is staring at your bishop on e5, but his king on g1 is boxed in and your rook on f2 sits close.

drills.title: vs 1asaka (728) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White wanted Re1, putting the rook on the e-file against your bishop on e5, and that bishop has no defender. a6 ignores the threat, and after Re1 Rde8 Bd6 your bishop retreats and White gets a free tempo for b3 and queenside space. Qf3 is the move because the queen from c6 strikes the rook on h1 along the diagonal and eyes the f2 pawn, so White has to deal with that before the rook can come to e1 with purpose. The line runs Qf3, Rd1, Rde8, Re1, Bd6, a4, and your queen stays active on the kingside while the bishop finds a safe square. The principle: when an enemy rook is heading for your file, look for a queen move that hits the rook first.
drills.threat: White's rook on h1 is ready to swing to e1 and hit your bishop on e5, which nothing is defending.

drills.coachNote: What Black wanted was Rc2+, the rook landing on c2 with check on your king on c1, protected by the bishop, and then grabbing the c3 pawn. Qxc4 wins the knight, but it leaves c2 and the king's shelter open, so Rc2+ Kb1 Rxc3+ Ka1 gives Black the initiative. You were already -6.7, and this costs about 4 pawns more. Qb3 is the answer because the queen attacks the knight on c4 and covers both c2 and b2 at once, so the check is gone. If Black trades with Rxb2 Qxb2 Nxb2 Kxb2, the queens are off and your king is safe on b2. The principle: before you grab material, check which checks your opponent gets after your queen leaves its current defensive post.

drills.coachNote: Black was lining up on the e-file, so your Be2 is effectively pinned to the king on e1 and every tempo matters. dxc5 looks like a simple pawn trade, but Black recaptures with the d6 pawn and opens the d-file for his queen, and after Bd3 you have to spend a move with Ng1 just to hold the bishop. You were already -1.9, and this costs about 2 more pawns. Kf1 is the answer because it steps off the e-file, unpinning Be2 and letting you move it without the king getting skewered. The line runs a6, Qd1, Qb6, Nb3, Nc6, and the game stays a fight with your bishop free. The principle: before you trade or push, check which of your pieces are pinned on a file and move the king out of the line first.
drills.threat: Black's rook on e8 is staring down the e-file at your Be2 and king on e1, and his bishop on f5 is aiming at d3.

drills.coachNote: White wanted to keep that knight on f5 as a thorn, hitting h6 and g7 while e4 makes it hard to chase away cheaply. b6 ignores the knight, so White retreats with Ng3, then Black's knight can reroute to d4 and the position loses its coordination. Bxf5 is the answer because your bishop on e6 trades for that annoying knight, and after exf5 Qd7 keeps your queen active and the pressure on. You were up about 1.7, and b6 drops you roughly 1.4 pawns. The principle: when an enemy piece sits defended by a pawn in your camp, trade it off with the piece that already attacks it rather than hoping it leaves.

drills.title: vs Abfab18 (791) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Black wanted his king to walk through f7 and f6 to attack your e5 and g5 pawns, so the race is about who gets their king to the right square first. Kf4 looks natural, but after Kf7 e4 Ke7 Ke3 your king has spent its moves in the wrong place while Black's king reaches the e-file. Kf3 is the answer because it keeps your king one step from e3, so e4 and Ke3 come without losing a tempo, and the line runs Kf7, e4, Ke7, Ke3, Kf7. You were winning at +19.8, and this throws away about 10.6 pawns of that. The principle: in king-and-pawn endings, count the king moves needed to reach the square your pawns require, and don't step into a file where the enemy king is coming.
drills.threat: Black's king on e7 is marching toward f6, where it would hit your e5 and g5 pawns at the same time.

drills.title: vs Abfab18 (791) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Black's plan is to walk the king from f7 through e7 toward d6, where it can start working on your e5 and c6 pawns. Bb3 retreats the bishop along the same a2 to g8 diagonal and spends a tempo while that king walks, so the eval slides from about +20 to about +10. This one is closer than the numbers suggest, since the engine also lists Bb3 as acceptable, but it still hands back ground in a race you were winning. Ba2 keeps the bishop on that diagonal without giving up the square, and it leaves your king free to walk to c4 and then b5 while the a4 and e3 pawns hold the queenside. The principle to carry: in a king race, don't spend a tempo on a retreat that the opponent's king will use.
drills.threat: Black's king is marching from f7 toward d6, and your bishop on c4 is what holds the d5 and e6 squares.

drills.title: vs osmanahma (728) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Black wants Qxd2 with mate, since the rook on f2 covers e2 and protects the queen, so your king can't recapture. Rf1 looks like it's attacking that rook, but it doesn't stop Qxd2, and after the queen lands on d2 your king has no squares left and the game is over from a position where you were already winning by about 5 pawns. Qd7+ answers the threat by checking on the seventh rank, which forces Black's king off f7 before anything else happens. After that, O-O-O puts your rook on d1 to cover the d2 square, and the line runs Kf6, O-O-O, Bh6, Kb1, with your king safely tucked away. The principle: when the opponent has a queen and rook aimed at one square, check first and count the mate before you make a quiet move.
drills.threat: Black's queen on g5 and rook on f2 are both lined up on your knight at d2, and your king on e1 has very few squares.

drills.coachNote: Black wants to meet your queen with Qd7 and force trades, and the rook on h5 is sitting in the open where your queen can reach it. Qd4 centralises but leaves the rook alone, so after Qd7 your bishop has to retreat to f4, and Black gets Qh7 and Qa4+ with tempo while you are still tidying up. You were already about 6 pawns up, and that gives away most of the easy conversion. Qg6+ is the answer because the check on the e8 king along the g6 to e8 diagonal comes first and forces Kd7, and then Qxh5 wins the rook on h5 outright. Next, Kc6 and Nd4+ keep the king under pressure while the extra material does the work. The principle to carry: when a check also attacks a loose piece, play the check first.
drills.threat: Black's rook on h5 is loose on the fifth rank, and your queen on d3 has a check that swings toward the kingside.

drills.coachNote: White wants b7 supported from the e6 rook, so the pawn promotes before your rook can get back. Rc4+ gives check along the fourth rank, but after Kd5 your rook has to move again, and the king is now attacking it from close range. You were already about 7 pawns down, so every tempo matters, and this one lets the b-pawn run. Rc1 is the answer because the rook drops behind the passed pawn and heads for b1. After b7, Re1+ and Rb1 stop the promotion on b8, and then Rc6 gets the rook into play. The principle: a rook belongs behind a passed pawn, so give checks only if they gain something.
drills.threat: White's a and b pawns are advancing together, and your rook on c5 is the only piece standing in front of them.

drills.coachNote: Black's problem is that b6 hits the rook on c7 with tempo, and the pawn push also frees the b-file for White's passer. Rc7 puts the rook exactly where that push hits it, and after b6 the rook has to run while White keeps pushing. You were about 6 pawns down, so this move gives up the last chance to make the position hard to win. Ra7 is the answer because the rook lands on the seventh rank, attacks the a6 pawn along the a-file, and still reaches a6 after b6 because the capture comes with the escape. The line from there is Re8, Kh5, Kd6, Kg5, and Rg8+ keeps your king active. The principle: put your rook where the pawn's next push can't attack it.
drills.threat: White's b5 pawn is ready to push, and the a6 pawn is weak on the a-file, so your rook on e7 has to pick its square carefully.

drills.coachNote: Black wants the bishop to reroute and free the king, and your king is currently the piece that decides whether the c-pawns get support. Kc6 puts the king in front of your own pawns with no real support role, and the game gets harder as Black's bishop comes out, which you can see in the eval swing from about +68 to much less. You were winning by a huge margin, so this move throws away almost the whole advantage. Kb4 is the answer because the king keeps watch on the c4 and c5 squares while your pawns advance. The line runs Bh3, Kc5, Kd8, Kd6, and Kc8, with your king heading for the centre while Black's king is kept in the corner. The principle: in a pawn ending, the king's job is to support the pawns, not to stand in front of them.
drills.threat: Black's bishop on f5 wants to reroute to g4, and your king on b5 needs a square that keeps the c-pawns protected.

drills.coachNote: Black wants Kxb6, winning your rook outright, since the rook on b6 has no defender on your side. Kb5 protects the rook by standing next to it, but it commits your king to the b-file and lets Black's bishop start its journey, which is why the eval falls from about +58 to much less. You were winning by a large margin, so the move gives away a lot. Rb2 is the answer because it takes the rook out of danger and keeps it working, and the line continues Bh3, Ka3, Bg4, Rh2, with the rook heading to the kingside to attack the bishop and the g6 pawn. The principle: when a piece is attacked and unprotected, move it to a useful square rather than defending it passively.
drills.threat: Black's king on c7 is attacking your rook on b6, and nothing currently protects that rook.

Rh7 attacks the queen on h6, but it leaves f8 with no defender, so Qxf8# follows and the game ends. You were around +6 and had the attacking chances, which is what makes this so painful. Qh7 is the answer: your queen goes to h7 in the diagonal from d3, offering a trade that forces Qxh7+ and Kxh7, and then Bf4 and Re8 trade down the rooks cleanly. The principle: before you play an attacking move, check which of your own pieces was guarding the back rank.
